title: Python Basics
blurb: Functions, parameters, return values, and the rules Python cares about.

sections.heading: What a function is
sections.body: A function is a named block of instructions you can run whenever you want, just by writing its name followed by parentheses. Think of it like a saved drone routine: instead of typing every command each time, you give the routine a name like takeoff_and_hover and just call it.
sections.code:
def announce():
    print("Drone ready for takeoff")

announce()
announce()
# prints "Drone ready for takeoff" twice

sections.heading: Parameters: giving a function information
sections.body:
A parameter is a placeholder name inside the parentheses of a function. It lets you pass in different values each time you call the function, instead of the function always doing the exact same thing.

In the example below, distance is a parameter. When we call the function, we plug in a real number, called an argument, for it.
sections.code:
def fly_forward(distance):
    print("Flying forward", distance, "cm")

fly_forward(50)
fly_forward(120)

sections.heading: Return: sending a value back
sections.body:
return hands a value back to whoever called the function, so it can be stored or used in more math. This is different from print, which only shows something on the screen but doesn't give the value to the rest of your program.

A function stops running the moment it hits a return statement, even if there is more code written below it.
sections.code:
def double_distance(distance):
    return distance * 2

result = double_distance(30)
print(result)   # 60
sections.note: Anything after a return inside the same block never runs, since the function has already exited.

sections.heading: A function with no return gives you None
sections.body: If a function never hits a return statement, Python quietly gives back a special value called None, which means "nothing here." This trips people up a lot: the function might print something useful, but if you try to use its result in math, you'll get an error or unexpected behavior because the result is actually None.
sections.code:
def log_landing():
    print("Drone has landed")
    # no return statement!

outcome = log_landing()
print(outcome)   # None
sections.note: If your function's job is to hand back an answer, always make sure it ends with a return.

sections.heading: Variables and calling functions
sections.body: A variable is a name that stores a value so you can use it again later. You can store the result of a function call in a variable, pass a variable in as an argument, or even use a variable's value inside a function.
sections.code:
battery = 80
speed = 40

def time_estimate(speed):
    return 100 // speed

minutes_left = time_estimate(speed)
print(minutes_left)   # 2

sections.heading: Indentation matters
sections.body: Python uses indentation (spaces at the start of a line) to know which lines belong inside a function, loop, or if statement. Other languages use curly braces {} for this, but Python uses the whitespace itself as part of the code's structure. Every line inside the same block must be indented by the same amount, usually 4 spaces.
sections.note: Mixing tabs and spaces, or indenting inconsistently, will cause an IndentationError.

sections.heading: Comments
sections.body: A comment starts with # and is ignored completely when the program runs. Comments are notes for humans reading the code, used to explain why something is done, not just what it does.

title: Strings
blurb: Text in Python: measuring it, slicing it, and looping through it.

sections.heading: len(): measuring a string
sections.body: A string is just text wrapped in quotes, like "TELLO-1234". The built-in function len() counts how many characters are in a string, including spaces and punctuation.
sections.code:
drone_name = "TELLO-1234"
print(len(drone_name))   # 10

sections.heading: Indexing: grabbing one character
sections.body: Every character in a string has a position number called an index, and counting starts at 0, not 1. So s[0] is the first character, and s[1] is the second one.
sections.code:
command = "forward"
print(command[0])   # f
print(command[3])   # w
sections.note: Trying to index past the end of the string, like s[100] on a short string, causes an IndexError.

sections.heading: Slicing: grabbing a chunk
sections.body: Slicing pulls out a piece of a string using s[start:stop]. It includes the character at start but stops right before the character at stop. You can also use negative numbers to count backward from the end, where -1 is the last character.
sections.code:
route = "NESW"
print(route[1:4])   # ESW
print(route[-1])    # W
print(route[:2])    # NE

sections.heading: Concatenation with +
sections.body: You can join two strings together with +. This is called concatenation. It only works between strings, so numbers need to be turned into text first with str() before joining them.
sections.code:
prefix = "TELLO-"
number = 42
full_name = prefix + str(number)
print(full_name)   # TELLO-42

sections.heading: The in keyword
sections.body: The in keyword checks whether one string appears anywhere inside another, and gives back True or False.
sections.code:
log = "battery low, landing now"
print("landing" in log)   # True
print("takeoff" in log)   # False

sections.heading: upper() and lower()
sections.body: .upper() and .lower() create a new copy of a string with every letter changed to uppercase or lowercase. This is handy for comparing text without worrying about how it was typed.
sections.code:
command = "Land"
print(command.upper())   # LAND
print(command.lower())   # land

sections.heading: Looping over a string, and immutability
sections.body: Since a string is a sequence of characters, you can loop over it with a for loop, one character at a time. Strings are also immutable, meaning once created, they can never be changed in place. Instead of editing a string, you always build a new one.
sections.code:
for letter in "UP":
    print(letter)
# prints U then P

s = "cat"
# s[0] = "b"   # this would raise an error, strings can't be edited
new_s = "b" + s[1:]
print(new_s)   # bat
sections.note: Because strings can't be changed in place, operations like upper() always return a brand new string instead of modifying the original.

title: Lists
blurb: Storing a bunch of values together, and the ways to loop through them.

sections.heading: What a list is, and len()
sections.body: A list holds multiple values in one ordered container, written with square brackets. Just like strings, you can use len() to find out how many items are in a list.
sections.code:
distances = [30, 60, 90, 120]
print(len(distances))   # 4

sections.heading: Indexing and slicing lists
sections.body: Lists use the same indexing and slicing rules as strings: positions start at 0, and list[start:stop] grabs a chunk without including the stop position.
sections.code:
waypoints = ["N", "E", "S", "W"]
print(waypoints[0])     # N
print(waypoints[1:3])   # ['E', 'S']
print(waypoints[-1])    # W

sections.heading: append(): adding to a list
sections.body: .append() adds a new item onto the end of a list. This changes the original list directly, it doesn't create a new one.
sections.code:
flight_log = ["takeoff"]
flight_log.append("forward 50")
flight_log.append("land")
print(flight_log)   # ['takeoff', 'forward 50', 'land']

sections.heading: Looping with for x in list
sections.body: The simplest way to visit every item in a list is for item in my_list:. Each time through the loop, item becomes the next value in the list, in order.

sections.heading: Looping by index with range(len(...))
sections.body: Sometimes you need to know the position of each item, not just its value, for example to compare an item with the one next to it. For that, loop over range(len(my_list)), which gives you the index numbers 0, 1, 2, ... to use with my_list[i].

sections.heading: Building a new list
sections.body: A very common pattern is to start with an empty list, then use a loop and .append() to fill it with new values based on another list, without changing the original one.
sections.code:
distances = [10, 20, 30]
doubled = []
for d in distances:
    doubled.append(d * 2)
print(doubled)   # [20, 40, 60]

sections.heading: Lists are mutable
sections.body: Unlike strings, lists are mutable, meaning you can change them in place after they're created. You can replace an item at a specific index, or use methods like .append(), all without making a brand new list.
sections.code:
route = ["N", "E", "S"]
route[1] = "NE"
print(route)   # ['N', 'NE', 'S']
sections.note: This is the opposite of strings, where s[0] = "x" would raise an error.

title: If and Boolean Logic
blurb: Making decisions in code with True, False, comparisons, and if statements.

sections.heading: True and False
sections.body: True and False are a special type of value in Python called a boolean. They represent yes/no or on/off answers, and they're written with a capital letter, unlike other languages.
sections.code:
battery_ok = True
print(battery_ok)   # True
print(type(battery_ok))   # <class 'bool'>

sections.heading: Comparison operators
sections.body: Comparison operators compare two values and produce a boolean. The most common ones are == (equal to), != (not equal to), >, <, >=, and <=. Notice that == has two equal signs, since a single = is used for assigning variables, not comparing them.
sections.code:
altitude = 120
print(altitude > 100)    # True
print(altitude == 120)   # True
print(altitude != 120)   # False

sections.heading: and, or, not
sections.body: These words combine or flip boolean values. and is true only when both sides are true. or is true when at least one side is true. not flips a value from true to false or false to true.
sections.code:
battery = 40
wind = False

can_fly = battery > 20 and not wind
print(can_fly)   # True

needs_landing = battery < 15 or wind
print(needs_landing)   # False

sections.heading: if, elif, and else
sections.body: An if statement runs a block of code only when its condition is True. elif (short for "else if") checks another condition if the first was false, and else catches everything that didn't match any condition above it.

sections.heading: Early return
sections.body: You can return as soon as you know the answer, instead of nesting more if statements below it. This is called an early return, and it often makes functions shorter and easier to read.
sections.note: Once a function hits return, it exits immediately, so later checks are simply skipped.

sections.heading: Returning a boolean directly
sections.body: A comparison like battery > 20 already produces True or False by itself. That means you can often skip writing if x: return True else: return False, and just return the comparison directly, since it's already the boolean you want.
sections.code:
def has_enough_battery(level):
    return level > 20

# instead of the longer version below:
# def has_enough_battery(level):
#     if level > 20:
#         return True
#     else:
#         return False

print(has_enough_battery(35))   # True
